query: We are investigating a specific eutectic high entropy alloy (comprising Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) that exhibits a dual-phase lamellar structure and suffers from catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility. The operating regime is room temperature uniaxial tension. Known failures include the strength-ductility trade-off and stress concentration at phase interfaces. Design constraints require maintaining the alloy composition while altering the microstructure to arrest interfacial cracking and promote uniform plasticity. Propose a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment hypothesis that could transform the lamellar structure into a patterned configuration, explain the predicted boundary conditions for success (e.g., specific temperature/pressure windows), and define a falsification experiment involving conventional hot isostatic pressing to isolate the effect of extreme pressure.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment (specifically, severe plastic deformation followed by high-pressure annealing) to the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will transform the continuous lamellar structure into a discontinuous, patterned (e.g., globularized or reticulated) configuration, thereby arresting interfacial cracking and promoting uniform plasticity at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine, regular, continuous lamellar structure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard B2 (NiAl-rich) phases.
generation.intervention: High-intensity thermomechanical treatment involving severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing) followed by annealing under high hydrostatic pressure (e.g., 10–20 GPa) to induce phase boundary restructuring without altering bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Temperature window: 600–900 °C (below the eutectic melting point but sufficient for diffusion); Pressure window: 10–20 GPa (sufficient to stabilize fcc or modify stacking fault energy); Strain rate: High (during deformation phase).
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of the continuous lamellar interface into a discontinuous, patterned network (e.g., globularized B2 particles within an fcc matrix or a reticulated inter-dendritic framework) that disrupts stress concentration paths and increases the density of dislocation storage sites.
generation.mechanism: The high hydrostatic pressure suppresses the formation of brittle interfacial cracks by altering the stacking fault energy and interfacial energy (similar to the pressure-induced stabilization of fcc phases observed in CoCrFeMnNi), while the thermomechanical strain breaks the continuity of the lamellae. This creates a patterned microstructure where the hard phase acts as a barrier to crack propagation (similar to the Laves phase reticulated structure in HfMoTaTiZr) rather than a continuous weak path, thereby enhancing strain hardening and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant increase in room temperature ductility (fracture strain > 15%) and a maintained or slightly improved ultimate tensile strength, with the σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio remaining high (>10) due to the enhanced strain hardening capacity of the new patterned microstructure, while catastrophic interfacial cracking is eliminated.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy with continuous lamellar structure, which exhibits high strength but catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility under room temperature uniaxial tension.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the pressure is sufficient to modify the phase boundary energy and stacking fault energy (e.g., >10 GPa) but does not induce a complete phase transformation to a single-phase structure (e.g., full fcc or full B2) that would eliminate the dual-phase strengthening mechanism. If pressure is too low (<5 GPa), the lamellar structure may remain continuous, failing to arrest cracking.
generation.uncertainty: The exact pressure threshold required to transform the lamellar structure into a patterned configuration without inducing a complete phase transformation is unknown. Additionally, the specific annealing time required to achieve the patterned state without coarsening the microstructure is uncertain. The mechanism relies on extrapolating pressure effects observed in CoCrFeMnNi (PMC5461481) and Laves phase reticulation in HfMoTaTiZr (PMC10759803) to the AlCoCrFeNi system, which may have different stacking fault energies and phase stability fields.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 samples: (1) As-cast (baseline), (2) Subjected to Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa (conventional HIP conditions), and (3) Subjected to the proposed high-intensity thermomechanical treatment (e.g., SPD + 15 GPa annealing). All samples will be tested under room temperature uniaxial tension.
measurements: Microstructural characterization via SEM and TEM to quantify lamellar continuity vs. patterned/globularized structure.
Room temperature tensile testing to measure Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS), Yield Strength (YS), and Fracture Strain.
In-situ XRD during deformation to monitor phase stability and stacking fault density.
Fracture surface analysis to identify crack initiation sites (interface vs. matrix).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) The high-intensity treatment fails to transform the lamellar structure into a discontinuous patterned configuration (i.e., lamellae remain continuous), OR (2) The high-intensity treatment results in a single-phase structure that eliminates the dual-phase strengthening mechanism, OR (3) The high-intensity treatment does not result in a statistically significant increase in fracture strain (>10% improvement) compared to the as-cast baseline, OR (4) The conventional HIP treatment (152 MPa) produces a similar microstructural transformation and mechanical improvement, indicating that the extreme pressure is not the critical factor.

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: HfMoTaTiZr refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA). Intervention: Addition of 4.2 at% Cr to the nominal composition. Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere, re-melted at least 5 times. Test conditions: Room temperature. Structure change: Formation of a Laves phase (Cr, Mo)2(Hf, Ti, Zr) in addition to the single-phase BCC structure; Laves phase forms a continuous reticulated inter-dendritic framework with a volume fraction of 3.8%. Property change: Hardness increased from 460.1 Hv 0.3 to 535.8 Hv 0.3 (56.96% higher); Yield strength increased from 1543.1 ± 40.9 MPa to 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa (207.5 MPa higher); Fracture strain increased from 11.6 ± 4.0% to 14.0 ± 2.9% (20.6% higher). Mechanism: Solid solution hardening due to Cr dissolution in BCC phase and lattice distortion; presence of hard intermetallic Laves phase; reticulated structure of Laves phase hinders crack propagation and compensates for plasticity loss. Evidence: measured. Quote: "4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase."

Intervention effect. Base system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (as-cast). Intervention: Analyzed strain hardening behavior via σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio. Processing: Tensile testing to determine proof stress and fracture stress. Test conditions: Room temperature. Property change: σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio close to 16, far beyond conventional alloys (range 1 ~ 3) and NiAl-based alloys (range 1 ~ 2). Mechanism: The very large strain hardening for the as-cast EHEA could originate from the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. Evidence: measured. Quote: "the EHEA has a σ UTS /σ 0.2 (note it is the proof stress here) close to 16"

Intervention effect. Base system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (as-cast). Intervention: Characterized phase constitution via XRD and DSC. Processing: XRD using Shimadzu XRD-6000 with Cu target (20°–100° 2θ, 4°/min); DSC using Netzsch STA 449 F3 (10 K/min heating/cooling). Test conditions: Room temperature (XRD); Ambient to 1450°C (DSC). Structure change: fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution; single melting event in DSC confirming eutectic composition. Mechanism: Correlating the compositional information and the XRD result, the A regions shall correspond to the fcc phase while the B regions (including B II ) to the B2 phase. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of the alloy is given in Fig. 3a , showing an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution"

Intervention effect. Base system: Retained hcp CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. Intervention: Heated to elevated temperatures at 6, 14, and 26 GPa. Processing: In situ laser heating XRD coupled with a DAC (double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating). Test conditions: Pressures of 6, 14, and 26 GPa; temperatures up to ~1,400 K. Structure change: Inverse transition from hcp back to fcc phase. Property change: Critical transition temperature for hcp-to-fcc transformation increased with pressure; at 26 GPa, transition started at ~1,400 K. Mechanism: Pressure increases the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transformation; fcc is stable at high temperatures and lower pressures. Evidence: measured. Quote: "With continuous heating above ∼1,400 K at 26 GPa, the fcc phase started to gradually grow at the expense of the hcp phase"

Intervention effect. Base system: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (fcc). Intervention: High pressure application. Processing: In situ high-pressure synchrotron XRD. Test conditions: Room temperature, pressure up to ~41 GPa. Structure change: fcc-to-hcp transition; hcp-(002) and hcp-(110) planes inherit fcc-(111) and fcc-(220) planes. Property change: No obvious volume collapse; bulk moduli of fcc and hcp are consistent with previous results. Mechanism: Transition involves stacking faults, dislocations, and twinning events; low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2) facilitates the transition. Evidence: measured. Quote: "It is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively"

Intervention effect. Base system: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy buttons prepared by vacuum arc melting. Intervention: Gravity casting followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). Processing: Vacuum arc melting, gravity casting into bars, HIP at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests, creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa. Structure change: Single-phase BCC before HIP; after HIP, a secondary HCP phase (ZrHf-rich) appeared, evenly dispersed in the matrix. Property change: Hardness increased from 323.5 ± 6.5 HV to 437.2 ± 11.6 HV; materials found to be highly brittle under tension with elongation below machine detection limit. Mechanism: The HIP process is responsible for the appearance of the HCP phase, likely due to slow cooling allowing eutectoid reaction or precipitation of HCP component from the BCC phase. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings."

Intervention effect. Base system: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy buttons prepared by vacuum arc melting. Intervention: Suction-assisted casting followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). Processing: Vacuum arc melting, suction-assisted casting using a vacuum pump, HIP at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests, creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa. Structure change: Single-phase BCC before HIP; after HIP, a secondary HCP phase (ZrHf-rich) appeared, concentrated mostly at the grain boundaries. Property change: Hardness increased from 330.2 ± 9.8 HV to 509.1 ± 13.5 HV; materials found to be highly brittle under tension with elongation below machine detection limit. Mechanism: The difference in hardness and microstructure may be related to the distribution of the ZrHf-rich phase, which is concentrated mainly at the grain boundaries in the suction-assisted casting. Evidence: measured. Quote: "Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C."

Intervention effect. Base system: PM CoCrFeMnNi in fcc and hcp phases. Intervention: Calculation of fcc-hcp interfacial energy (σ) using the Olson and Cohen model and supercell approach. Processing: Comparison of σ derived from LSF and FS schemes with experimental lattice expansion. Test conditions: Temperature interval 300–900 K; extrapolation to 0 K. Structure change: LSFs slightly lower the interfacial energy σ compared to FS calculations. Property change: LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m^-2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K; σ predicted to be ~6.1 mJ m^-2 at 0 K in LSF vs 7.0 mJ m^-2 in FS. Mechanism: The role of LSFs disclosed in PM CoCrFeMnNi is in good agreement with that reported in PM γ-Fe and Fe-22.5 at.% Mn. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "It is evident from Fig. 4 that the LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m −2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K."
